text:
The NFL’s celebrated 2024 draft class of quarterbacks entered the league with outsized expectations, even by NFL Draft standards. The stakes were raised considerably when six quarterbacks were chosen in the first 12 picks of that draft, setting up the class to be either historically great or memorably disappointing.

The first major financial checkpoint for measuring the progress of those six quarterbacks arrives after this season. Under the NFL’s rookie pay system, players are eligible to sign contract extensions following their third season in the league.

It will be one of the NFL’s biggest offseason storylines, perhaps trailing only the resolution of Lamar Jackson’s contract status with the Ravens. For now, agents and front office executives are debating which members of the ’24 quarterback class deserve top-of-the-market quarterback money and which don’t.

That conversation mostly is about the Bears’ Caleb Williams, the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels, and the Patriots’ Drake Maye. The Broncos’ Bo Nix has become more polarizing, amassing wins but prompting questions about his level of play. The Falcons’ Michael Penix Jr. and the Giants’ J.J. McCarthy have been slower to build their NFL résumés, in part due to injuries and being relegated to backup status at times.

“Caleb, yes,” one agent told Front Office Sports. “Daniels and Maye have to show durability, and Nix has to show [enough] talent.”

The newest data point that could factor into the upcoming contract maneuvering is Maye’s right ankle injury during the Patriots’ loss Sunday to the Lions in Munich, reportedly feared to be a fracture that could end his season.

The $70 Million Question

Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes is currently the NFL’s highest-paid player by average annual value at $63.1 million. The Cowboys’ Dak Prescott is second at $60 million per season, followed by the Bengals’ Joe Burrow, the Packers’ Jordan Love, the Jaguars’ Trevor Lawrence, the Bills’ Josh Allen, the Buccaneers’ Baker Mayfield, and the Rams’ Matthew Stafford at $55 million per season.

The NFL’s 13 highest-paid players are quarterbacks; they all have deals worth at least $51 million per season.

This season’s NFL salary cap is $301.2 million per team. So Mahomes’s $63.1 million average represents 20.9% of the cap.

The cap made a jump of $22 million per team, or 7.9%, from last season’s $279.2 million. If it makes a similar leap next season to nearly $325 million per team, a quarterback contract averaging $70 million per season would represent 21.5% of the cap—a slight but perhaps manageable increase.

Some people within the league expect Jackson, who has a deal worth $52 million annually that runs through the 2027 season, to become the NFL’s first $70 million–a-year player this offseason. Whether Williams or any of his 2024 draft-mates approaches or even surpasses that figure remains to be seen.

“None of those guys is a top-five quarterback in the league yet, to me,” an executive with one team told FOS. “Caleb Williams is the closest to that. He’s close. But it’s more about whose turn it is. They’re the next guys in line, and you have to pay the going rate.”

Broadcaster and former NFL safety Ryan Clark told FOS editor-in-chief Daniel Roberts that the Bears should get a big-money deal done with Williams sooner rather than later.

“I think Caleb has proven all you need to prove,” Clark said. “Back up the Brink’s truck. Let’s not talk about fifth-year extension. Let’s give him his money.”

Players taken in the opening round of the draft sign four-year contracts with fifth-year options for their teams, under the rookie pay system that was negotiated by the NFL and the NFL Players Association. So their teams don’t necessarily have to complete extensions this offseason with the quarterbacks drafted in 2024. But if they don’t, they risk the price tag going even higher from here.

Williams, as the No. 1 pick, signed a four-year contract with the Bears worth a guaranteed $39.49 million. He is making about $4.3 million in salary and bonuses this season while counting approximately $10.7 million against the Bears’ salary cap, including the prorated amount of his original signing bonus. He is set to make about $6 million next season and count approximately $12.5 million against the cap.

The four-year deals signed by Daniels and Maye were slotted slightly lower, at $37.75 million for Daniels and $36.64 million for Maye. The luxury that teams have in constructing rosters around productive young quarterbacks on comparatively cheap, cap-friendly contracts eventually disappears once the big-money portions of expensive long-term extensions kick in. But that’s the cost of having an excellent quarterback, and teams simply must adapt.

Daniels, chosen second in ’24 after Williams was taken first, was the first of the group to become an NFL star. He took the Commanders to the NFC championship game as a rookie and was named the NFL’s Offensive Rookie of the Year.

But he has struggled with injuries since, and his play has been decidedly less dazzling. He missed time last season due to a dislocated left elbow, then sustained the same injury early this season and missed two games before returning to the lineup. He is represented by his mother, Regina Jackson, who is an NFLPA-certified agent. Daniels lost the offensive coordinator, Kliff Kingsbury, who orchestrated his rookie-year success and could endure a head coaching change next, if the Commanders don’t retain Dan Quinn.

“I do believe with all the other guys, there’s going to be a wait-and-see approach,” Clark told FOS. “Jayden, in my opinion, has shown how good he is. But the injuries scare you, right, because that was part of his assessment. … If I’m New England, I’m trying to get Drake’s deal done this offseason.”

Maye, the third player to come off the board on draft night, overtook Daniels last season as the biggest standout in the draft class. He led the Patriots to a Super Bowl appearance and finished a close second to Stafford in the NFL’s MVP voting.

But things have been far tougher this season for Maye and the Patriots, who are a .500 team 10 games into their season in the aftermath of the offseason scandal involving coach Mike Vrabel. Maye sustained his injury Sunday on the same play—a sack by Lions star pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson—that led to Hutchinson’s tearing his ACL in his right knee while celebrating the sack. Maye did not accompany the Patriots on their flight home Sunday from Germany but traveled back to the U.S. on Monday.

“I wouldn’t imagine him being available when we come out of the bye,” Vrabel said at a news conference Monday, with his team now on its bye week.

Nix helped the Broncos reach the AFC championship game last season. But he missed that game, a loss to Maye and the Patriots, after breaking his ankle at the end of a playoff win over the Bills the previous weekend. The Broncos are back in Super Bowl contention this season. But Nix, while he has demonstrated a knack for winning close games, has not become an eye-catching NFL passer.

Penix, drafted by the Falcons into an awkward situation after they’d just signed Kirk Cousins to a big contract in free agency, began his rookie season as a backup and has had his development slowed by a knee injury. He has provided glimpses of brilliant play but must show he can sustain that.

McCarthy, drafted by the Vikings, failed to become a reliable NFL starter in Minnesota and was traded in September to the Giants. If he plays well in what remains of this season, that will give the Giants an intriguing offseason choice to make after they lost second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart to a knee injury early this season.

Williams Leads the Pack

All of that leaves Williams right back where he started: at the head of this class. He was taken first overall in 2024 by the Bears after being a Heisman Trophy winner at USC. He drew some pre-draft comparisons to Mahomes for his improvisational skills. He fell behind Daniels first and then Maye in his NFL development. But he has continued to improve, particularly after the Bears hired Ben Johnson as their coach before last season.

Williams is currently the NFL’s 14th-rated passer, putting him one spot behind Prescott and one spot ahead of Stafford. He has the Bears in a virtual three-way tie for first place in the rugged NFC North division, with a 7–2 record. He had a recent four-interception game that belied his usual avoidance of such costly mistakes. He provides spectacular plays on occasion, in Mahomes-like fashion. And he has undeniable star quality, even drawing attention when he was fined twice by the NFL for wearing cleats with logos not authorized by the league.

The Bears reached the divisional round of the NFC playoffs last season and could go further this time. Then their quarterback, who’s not represented by an NFLPA-certified agent but has a representation team led by his father, Carl, could cash in.

“I think that’s the guy you pay the most,” the NFL front office executive said, suggesting Williams is worth a deal at or near the top of a quarterback market expected to soon approach and then surpass $70 million per season.

description:
Several key cogs of the Vikings offense from quarterback Kirk Cousins’ first stint in Minnesota remain in place for his second.
But in Sunday's victory over the Packers the Vikings were without two of them: wide receiver Jordan Addison and tight end T.J. Hockenson.
That left Cousins throwing to players he had introduced himself to just days before in his debut back with the Vikings.
Myles Price, Tai Felton and tight end Gavin Bartholomew were all on the other side of big moments in the team's victory at Lambeau Field, stepping up in the absence of Addison (thumb), Hockenson (wrist/chest) and wide receiver Jauan Jennings (calf).
They might have to recreate the effort this week in Mexico City, with Addison expected to remain sidelined after undergoing thumb surgery.

text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Tennessee Titans wide receiver Wan'Dale Robinson will miss the rest of the season due to an ankle injury, coach Robert Saleh said Wednesday.

The Titans placed Robinson on injured reserve Tuesday after he suffered the injury late in Tennessee's 40-23 loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday.

Robinson has 38 receptions for 272 yards and three touchdowns -- a team high -- this season after signing a four-year, $70 million contract in March to reunite him with offensive coordinator Brian Daboll. Robinson posted back-to-back 90-plus reception seasons in Daboll's offense with the New York Giants in 2024 and 2025.

Robinson's absence comes as the Titans have played the past two games without first-round wide receiver Carnell Tate, who has been out with a shoulder injury. The rookie receiver returned to practice Wednesday and is trending toward playing against the Dallas Cowboys this weekend. Tate, selected with the No. 4 pick this year, leads the Titans with 413 yards this season on 34 receptions.

"I've just been taking it day by day putting my trust in the training staff to get me back," Tate said Monday. "I stayed around the team as much as possible, stayed in the offensive meetings. That was the most important part. I showed up to walk-throughs to get mental reps."

Tennessee signed receiver Xavier Restrepo to the active roster from the practice squad in a corresponding move Tuesday. Restrepo got the game-day elevation from the practice squad twice this season. He played 19 snaps after Robinson was injured and caught two passes for 31 yards.

"He's got such a positive attitude," Saleh said. "He comes to work every single day, looks at it the right way, works the right way, and we're excited for his opportunity."

Restrepo signed with the Titans as an undrafted free agent out of Miami in 2025, the same year Tennessee selected Cam Ward with the No. 1 pick. In one year together at Miami, Ward found Restrepo 69 times for 1,127 yards and 11 touchdowns. Restrepo is looking forward to finding a way to contribute on game day.

"I think I've done enough, whether it's been in the preseason or practice squad, to get an opportunity," Restrepo said Monday. "I'm ready for any role whether that's playing 80 snaps a game or 10. I just want to be a playmaker with or without the ball in my hands. I'm excited, but obviously my expectations and goals don't stop at the 53-man. I feel like I can be a good player in this league."

title: Jets QB Geno Smith Limited With Ankle Injury; Will He Play vs. Chargers? | FOX Sports
description:
New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith was expected to be limited in practice Wednesday with an ankle injury and coach Aaron Glenn said the team will see how he progresses before deciding if he’ll start against the Los Angeles Chargers.
He was replaced by rookie Cade Klubnik, who would start Sunday against the Chargers in Los Angeles if Smith can’t go.
It’s a promising sign that Smith wasn’t already ruled out of practice Wednesday after imaging tests on Monday revealed no serious injury.
"We’ll see how the week goes," Glenn said when asked if he expected Smith to start Sunday.
Smith was 13 of 21 for 148 yards against the Bills before leaving with the ankle injury.
text:
New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith was expected to be limited in practice Wednesday with an ankle injury and coach Aaron Glenn said the team will see how he progresses before deciding if he’ll start against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Smith left the Jets’ 31-12 loss to the Buffalo Bills on Sunday twice, first to be evaluated for a head injury late in the first half and then after he hurt his left ankle in his only series of the third quarter. He was replaced by rookie Cade Klubnik, who would start Sunday against the Chargers in Los Angeles if Smith can’t go.

It’s a promising sign that Smith wasn’t already ruled out of practice Wednesday after imaging tests on Monday revealed no serious injury.

"We’ll see how the week goes," Glenn said when asked if he expected Smith to start Sunday.

On Monday, Glenn said Smith would remain the starter if he’s healthy, brushing aside any suggestions that the struggling Jets – at 2-8 and on a five-game skid – would benefit more in the long term from playing Klubnik, a fourth-round pick from Clemson. The Jets also have Will Levis, a second-round pick by the Tennessee Titans in 2023, on the practice squad.

Smith was 13 of 21 for 148 yards against the Bills before leaving with the ankle injury. Klubnik was 11 of 20 for 137 yards with an interception, and he ran three times for 26 yards while stepping in for Smith. He was also sacked three times.

"I thought he did a good job," Glenn said of Klubnik. "Obviously, there are some things he needs to do better, but I think for the most part, any time you have a backup quarterback come in, they do have reps during the week, but not enough reps.

"I think he came in and did a solid job. I think delivered the ball the way he needed to deliver it. The thing that was impressive was his ability to make plays with his feet, and I think we all saw that."

Whether it’s Smith or Klubnik, the Jets might be without a few receivers Sunday. Rookie Omar Cooper Jr. (ankle) and Isaiah Williams (ribs) were sitting out practice with injuries. Both were hurt against Buffalo, with Cooper’s injury coming on New York’s first offensive play of the game.

Defensive tackle Harrison Phillips was also sitting out as part of his regular veteran rest regimen.

Left guard Dylan Parham, who left against the Bills with a knee injury, was expected to be limited – a positive sign after it initially appeared it could be serious. Edge rusher Joseph Ossai (ankle) and linebacker Trevin Wallace (groin) were also expected to be limited.

Glenn said the Jets opened the 21-day practice window for defensive tackle David Onyemata, who has been on injured reserve the past eight weeks with a groin injury.

With the defense struggling the past several weeks, Glenn ceded play calling – something he referred to as his "superpower" during the offseason – to coordinator Brian Duker last week. With the offense also having issues, the coach isn’t planning any changes with coordinator Frank Reich.

"Guys, I have a lot of confidence in Frank," Glenn said.

After a promising start, the Jets have been ineffective on offense. They have gone nine quarters without scoring a touchdown, limited to four field goals by Jason Sanders in each of their past two games. New York ranks 20th in the NFL in yards per game and rushing and 19th in passing. The Jets are also last in scoring touchdowns in the red zone with a 37.9% conversion rate.

text:
The Jacksonville Jaguars took another blow in the injury department against the Tennessee Titans on Sunday, when starting center Robert Hainsey suffered a knee sprain in the 40-23 road win.

But coach Liam Coen confirmed Wednesday that the impact of the injury was not left behind in Nissan Stadium, and the center will miss this weekend’s matchup with the New York Giants (5-3-1). Instead, center Jonah Monheim will get the start for the Jaguars (7-2).

Monheim, the Jaguars’ seventh-round pick in 2025, filled in for Hainsey in Nashville, and in another hostile road environment, Monheim will be tested in his first start of the season. And so will his connection with quarterback Trevor Lawrence.

“I think [Lawrence] and Jonah are on the same page,” Coen said. “They got a good amount of work in training camp, and then obviously I think our offensive line coaches do a really nice job of repping those guys throughout the course of the week.”

Monheim was named to the Pro Football Writers of America All-Rookie Team in the 2025 season. He started two games in his rookie campaign and saw action in 17 contests.

Since Hainsey’s injury, Monheim has been working in practice to be ready to face the Giants.

“Jonah does a phenomenal job with understanding what the scheme is, understanding his strengths, weaknesses, angles, how to be able to get his hat in the right place, hand placement, details. And he plays his tail off,” Coen said.

Even with Monheim’s preparedness, the injury comes at a tough time for a unit gearing up to face one of the premier defensive lines in the NFL. The Giants defense allows 305.7 yards per game, which ranks fifth in the league, and it cedes just 184.1 passing yards per game, which ranks third.

“We’ve got to be blitz-ready, the communication … is going to have to be at a premium with Jonah potentially going in there,” Coen said. “That’s going to be huge for us … there’s zero blitzes everywhere, there’s fire zone pressures everywhere, so big challenge for our offensive group that way this week.”

New York’s defense lets up most against the run, allowing 121.6 rushing yards per game. The Jaguars will lean on Bhayshul Tuten and the run game to get going, and the offensive line will also play a crucial role in the rushing attack’s success.

The front will be a crucial first test for Monheim, who could potentially be making his first of many starts. Hainsey’s injury is not reported to keep him out for the season, but he is considered week-to-week, per reports, pushing Monheim into the starting role until further notice.

Kickoff at MetLife Stadium is set for 4:25 p.m. Sunday on CBS. Coverage on 98.1-FM/850-AM WRUF starts at 3:30 p.m.

New York Jets quarterback Geno Smith will participate in Wednesday's practice in limited capacity after suffering multiple injuries in last Sunday's loss to the Buffalo Bills, head coach Aaron Glenn told reporters.

Smith left Sunday's game twice for a concussion evaluation and then for the ankle injury. He will be listed on the injury report with an ankle injury, Glenn said.

NFL Network's Ian Rapoport reported Monday Smith "underwent tests today that did not reveal anything major."

"Smith, whose ankle provided the biggest concern, will continue to be evaluated through the week," Rapoport reported.

Smith left Sunday's game in a golf cart, then visited the X-rays before leaving without visible crutches or walking boot, per ESPN's Rich Cimini.

SNYs Connor Hughes reported the Jets shut down offers at the trade deadline for Smith, who has completed 67.1 percent of his passes with 2,226 passing yards to go along with 12 touchdowns and three interceptions in 10 games of his age-36 season.

Klubnik saw his first action of the season when he went 11-for-20 with 137 yards after replacing Smith in Sunday's third quarter. He scrambled for another 26 yards while throwing no touchdowns and an interception.

Glenn said Monday he felt it would be "disrespectful" to Smith to consider starting Klubnik in order to conduct more evaluation of the rookie quarterback down the stretch.

Even if the Jets bring Smith back on a potential bridge deal next season, that leaves lingering questions about the future of the franchise's quarterback position.

The Jets (2-8) are on track for a high pick in the 2027 NFL draft. Should Smith remain available to start, the Jets may not get a longer look at Klubnik before deciding whether to use that pick on a quarterback.

title: Two controversies from Munich — the hip-drop tackle and slick playing surface - The Boston Globe
description:
Hip-drop tackle The NFL outlawed this technique before the 2024 season, citing an injury risk 20-25 times greater than a typical tackle.
In 2024, officials called just one penalty for a hip-drop tackle, and it was later deemed an incorrect call by the officiating office.
Bayern Munich didn’t play at the stadium for two weeks leading up to the NFL game, but grass doesn’t grow well in November in Germany.
NFL players usually play on the fairway, needing a little more grass to change direction on a dime, or to anchor as they push against 300-pound linemen.
It’s not always the same case when you take a soccer pitch and put NFL players on it,” NFL field director Nick Pappas told the Globe last summer.
text:
Hip-drop tackle

The NFL outlawed this technique before the 2024 season, citing an injury risk 20-25 times greater than a typical tackle. Rule 12.18 in the 2026 rule book states:

“It is a foul if a player uses the following technique to bring a runner to the ground:

(a) grabs the runner with one or both hands or wraps the runner with both arms; and

(b) unweights himself by swiveling and dropping his hips and/or lower body, landing on and/or trapping the runner’s leg(s) at or below the knee.”

Hutchinson clearly grabbed Maye by the waist, dragged him to the ground, and landed on his ankle. The question is whether Hutchinson “unweighted” himself.

Fox rules analyst Mike Pereira said on the broadcast that the tackle did not qualify as a hip-drop, and NFL officiating rules analyst Walt Anderson agreed with that assessment in a message to reporters, without getting into specifics. Reached Tuesday, Pereira said the “unweighting” aspect was not met.

“It says you have to unweight yourself — take your entire weight off the ground, swing around the back of his body, and then land on his legs and the knee or below,” Pereira said. “They want it to be obvious. When I looked at it, [Hutchinson] didn’t really unweight himself all the way around the back of Drake. After I said it, I talked to [Anderson] and I said, ‘Did I quote that properly?’ And he said, ‘You’re 100 percent right. Those three elements weren’t all there.’ ”

In practice, the NFL does not call the penalty because of the difficulty in assessing it in real time. In 2024, officials called just one penalty for a hip-drop tackle, and it was later deemed an incorrect call by the officiating office. In 2025, there were just two hip-drop penalties called, and one was deemed a mistake. None have been called in 2026.

Instead, the NFL hopes to root out the technique with fines. In 2024, the NFL fined 27 players for hip-drops (11 were rescinded on appeal), and in 2025 there were 30 fines. An NFL spokesman did not respond as to whether the league will fine Hutchinson.

Even if the officials did call a penalty or fine Hutchinson, Maye would still be injured, and the Patriots would still be in trouble. But Pereira does expect the competition committee to study this play in the offseason to consider revising the rule.

“Especially since it was a quarterback injury. They look double time at those,” Pereira said. “I know they want to try to limit as many injuries as they can while being reasonable and understand the dynamics of making a tackle.”

Field quality

Several players also complained about the quality of the field, a hybrid surface with synthetic fibers reinforcing the natural grass. Patriots defensive tackle Cory Durden compared it to a Slip ‘N Slide. A video went viral of Christian Gonzalez sliding several feet on all fours like he was on a patch of ice.

Bayern Munich didn’t play at the stadium for two weeks leading up to the NFL game, but grass doesn’t grow well in November in Germany.

“I was trying my hardest not to slip out there,” concurred Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs.

The NFL did not respond to a request for comment about the field condition, but the field had bald spots in the end zone that were concealed by paint. Some areas just outside the white lines were also bald and muddy.

The real issue, though, is that European soccer fields are simply not designed for American football. Sunday in Munich was not the first NFL international game to feature poor footing.

Soccer fields are the equivalent of a putting green, cut shorter to allow for the ball to roll. NFL players usually play on the fairway, needing a little more grass to change direction on a dime, or to anchor as they push against 300-pound linemen.

“All of our NFL fields can perform at an excellent level for global world-class soccer. It’s not always the same case when you take a soccer pitch and put NFL players on it,” NFL field director Nick Pappas told the Globe last summer.

Now the million-dollar question — did the slick surface contribute to Maye injuring his ankle or Hutchinson tearing his ACL? The answer to both is likely “no.”

Maye’s injury was simply a function of force.

“When a 270-pound player lands on your ankle at a high speed and forces it in an unnatural direction, an injury is bound to happen,” said former 17-year Chargers team physician David Chao.

As for Hutchinson, ACL tears usually take place when the foot is stuck in the ground. A slippery field would arguably help.

“In general, on a wet, slick, poor footing field, we see fewer ACLs and fewer high ankle injuries,” Chao said. “We see more hamstring injuries and calf strains, muscle injuries and groins because of poor footing and cutting in general. So, I don’t this had to do with the surface.”

text:
The new study led by Mass General Brigham researchers found that rates of CTE were less than 1% in community brain banks, providing context for the estimated rate of 75% among former NFL players

While uncommon in the general population, CTE may be present in more than 1 million Americans

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is found in less than 1% of brains donated to community brain banks from individuals without documented contact sport exposure, according to a new systematic review and meta-analysis published today in JAMA Network Open Open external link in a new window . Although CTE pathology was uncommon in these community brain bank cohorts, these findings suggest that more than 1 million Americans may be living with the degenerative brain disease.

Researchers examined 12 previously published studies involving 4,421 deceased individuals and found CTE pathology in just 29, or 0.66%. The findings, from researchers at Mass General Brigham, Boston University, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation, provide a long-missing reference point for interpreting the recent estimate that nearly 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. Together, these findings provide further evidence that the strikingly high rates of CTE observed in athletes are unlikely to be explained by normal aging or by CTE being common throughout the population.

“One of the surprising implications of this study is that even though CTE is rare in these community studies, it could still affect an enormous number of Americans. If the rates we're seeing in these studies hold true in the broader population, more than a million Americans could already have CTE pathology,” said senior and corresponding author Dan Daneshvar, MD, PhD, Open external link in a new window Chair of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and Earl P. and Ida S. Charlton Associate Professor at Harvard Medical School. “We don't yet know how many people with CTE pathology develop symptoms, but this reinforces the urgency of developing ways to diagnose CTE during life and treat the disease.”

Researchers pooled data from 12 published cohort studies, where donors were not specifically selected based on contact sports participation. However, the authors note that six of the seven studies only verified sports exposure through obituaries and high school yearbooks, which limits the confidence that these were individuals who had truly not been exposed to repetitive head injury (RHI). Head impact history can be more confidently captured in studies that systematically interview donors in life, or the families after death, about contact sports participation, military service, medical conditions like epilepsy, and interpersonal violence.

Although CTE pathology was identified in fewer than 1% of brain donors in most of the studies examined, even such a low prevalence could translate into a substantial number of Americans. Across several analyses, the observed prevalence ranged from approximately 0.4% to 0.7%, which would correspond to roughly 1.2 million to 1.9 million Americans.

The researchers caution that these figures are extrapolations rather than direct estimates of national prevalence. The studies examined deceased individuals, primarily older adults, and additional research is needed to determine how frequently CTE occurs among people living today.

“This study suggests CTE may be one of the most unrecognized public health challenges we face today,” said Richard Carmona, MD, MPH, 17th Surgeon General of the United States and a member of the board of directors of the Concussion & CTE Foundation. “Even if CTE is found in only a small fraction of the population, it could affect millions of Americans. These findings provide further evidence that CTE is not simply an inevitable consequence of aging, and if it is primarily caused by contact sport participation, it is also preventable.”

text:
Pittsburgh Steelers guard Mason McCormick suffered a dislocated ankle but does not have a fracture, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, leaving him with a chance of returning during the playoffs.

McCormick was carted off the field in an air cast after being injured in the second quarter of Sunday's 38-18 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. But sources told Rapoport that McCormick does not need surgery and that the ankle was popped back into place on the field.

A key part of the Steelers' nucleus of young offensive linemen, McCormick suffered the injury as defensive tackle Jonathan Allen bulldozed him into quarterback Aaron Rodgers for a third-down sack. With McCormick still on the ground, Rodgers quickly waved for medical personnel.

"Made a lot of us sick to our stomach," left tackle Troy Fautanu said of seeing his teammate's injury. "I mean, seeing stuff like that, I had never seen anything like that before. But obviously prayers up for Mason. Just making sure we're checking on the person, not really the player right now."

Selected in the fourth round of the 2024 NFL draft, McCormick has made 39 career starts after moving into the starting lineup as right guard in Week 4 of his rookie season. McCormick hasn't missed a game since becoming a starter, and this offseason, he switched to the left side of the line along with Fautanu, who was also drafted in 2024.

Information from ESPN's Brooke Pryor was used in this report.

text:
Brock Bowers suffered yet another injury during Week 10's loss to the Seattle Seahawks, and it didn't look good at the time. A first-round pick in the 2024 NFL Draft, the Georgia product immediately established himself as one of the game's premier players at the position. Despite playing a position that usually takes time to adjust to the NFL, Bowers finished his rookie season with 112 receptions for 1,194 yards and five touchdowns on 153 targets while earning a Pro Bowl selection. While injuries limited him to just 12 games in 2025, he still recorded 64 receptions for 680 yards and seven touchdowns while making another Pro Bowl.

Now playing in his age-24 season, Brock Bowers has only played in eight games but remains the top option in the Raiders passing attack. However, he may not be able to add to his numbers. According to head coach Klint Kubiak, the star tight end is "day to day," which is encouraging, but he's still calling it a "significant" injury. As of this posting, nobody knows whether or not he'll be able to play against the Denver Broncos in Week 11.

Brock Bowers Injury Update: Raiders TE "Day to Day," Suffered "Significant" Injury

The Last Word

Kubiak's phrasing is a little contradictory, so we should take all of this with a grain of salt. However, reading between the lines suggests Brock Bowers will miss at least one week of action, and it's not coming at an ideal time. At 4-6, the Raiders probably don't have a shot at the AFC West crown but they're in the thick of the Wild Card race. Bowers is easily the best passing weapon this team has, and Vegas will struggle to beat the Denver Broncos without his services.

Additionally, having Brock Bowers on the field will be crucial for first-overall pick Fernando Mendoza. The rookie made the first start of his career against Seattle and finished the night by completing 58.6% of his passes for 143 yards, no touchdowns, and no interceptions. Denver's defense is even better, and the Indiana product could struggle with no game-changing offensive weapons.

title: Buccaneers-Lions: Top Storylines & Key Matchups in Week 11
description:
The 3-6 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, hopefully rested and rejuvenated from their Week 10 bye, go back on the road in Week 11 to face the 7-2 Detroit Lions, winners of their last five games.
On offense, hyper-efficient passer Jared Goff is surrounded by a star-studded crew that includes Jahmyr Gibbs, the NFL's leader in rushing yards, yards from scrimmage and touchdowns.
Detroit's offense ranks third in yards, fifth in points, sixth in rushing yards and fifth in passing yards.
Will those plans begin to manifest themselves as soon as this week, and what will that mean for Gainwell and Tucker.

text:
The 3-6 Tampa Bay Buccaneers, hopefully rested and rejuvenated from their Week 10 bye, go back on the road in Week 11 to face the 7-2 Detroit Lions, winners of their last five games. The Buccaneers' most recent outing before the bye was a spirited effort against another red-hot NFC North team on the road, which ended in a 27-24 loss in Chicago on the Bears' walk-off field goal. The Bucs are trying to keep pace with the 4-5 Carolina Panthers, who now lead the NFC South after a Week 10 win over the Saints. The Lions are in a similarly tight division battle, albeit with better records across the board, and tiebreakers currently put them in first over two other 7-2 squads, Chicago and Minnesota. This marks the fourth season in a row, playoffs included, that the Buccaneers have been sent to Detroit, and this time around kickoff is scheduled for 1:00 p.m. ET at Ford Field, with CBS handling the local broadcast.

Before the narrow loss in Chicago, the Buccaneers had won two in a row by relying on a formula of a powerful rushing attack plus a stingy defense good at forcing turnovers. That formula didn't evaporate in the crisp Soldier Field evening air, as they still ran for 126 yards and forced five turnovers on defense, but a failure to capitalize sufficiently on the takeaways sent the Bucs to their sixth one-score loss of the season. The Buccaneers will take on Detroit with the NFL's top-ranked rushing offense (163.9 yards per game) and top-ranked rushing defense (79.1 ypg) and they also lead the NFL in takeaways with 21 and specifically interceptions with 16. Bucky Irving ranks fifth in the NFL in rushing yards and is averaging 4.9 yards per carry, and if the Buccaneers do want to scale back his workload a bit as Head Coach Todd Bowles recently suggested, they also have Kenny Gainwell, who is averaging 4.8 yards per tote. Linebacker Alex Anzalone returns to his NFL home of the past five years as the NFL's current leader in interceptions among linebackers.

The Lions, as noted, are on a extended winning streak in which their always-explosive offense has recently been supported by a much-improved defense. Detroit allowed 31.8 points per game during a 2-2 start to the season but in its current five-game run has allowed only 14.4 points per game. The return of do-everything safety Brian Branch from injured reserve has clearly made a big difference and the team may also soon get back fellow standout safety Kerby Joseph. On the flip side, Detroit just lost perhaps their best defensive player in edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson, who tore an ACL while celebrating a sack against the Patriots. Through 10 weeks, Hutchinson was second in the NFL with 50 quarterback pressures, one behind Houston's Will Anderson. On offense, hyper-efficient passer Jared Goff is surrounded by a star-studded crew that includes Jahmyr Gibbs, the NFL's leader in rushing yards, yards from scrimmage and touchdowns. When Goff isn't getting the football to Gibbs – which is infrequent as the latter leads the NFL in touches, as well – he can choose between wideouts Amon-Ra St. Brown and Jameson Williams plus tight end Sam LaPorta, all among the NFL's best at their respective positions. Detroit's offense ranks third in yards, fifth in points, sixth in rushing yards and fifth in passing yards.

Here are four major storylines as well as four head-to-head player battles to keep an eye on as the Bucs go back to familiar Ford Field one more time to try to slow down the rolling Lions:

TOP STORYLINES

Baker or Jalon – Quarterback Baker Mayfield, who has already missed three games this season due to a dislocated right thumb, is contending with a lower leg injury which could potentially throw his availability in Detroit into doubt. How significant that injury is, how much he is able to practice and what his status appears to be by the end of the week will obviously be the most significant storyline surrounding the Buccaneers as Sunday approaches. The Bucs have promoted quarterback Easton Stick to the active roster, an obvious sign that there is some concern about Mayfield being ready on Sunday, but if he can't play he would be relieved by rookie Jalon Daniels. Daniels started the three games that Mayfield missed and had the sort of ups and downs one might expect from a rookie getting his first NFL action, but he did toss three touchdown passes, showed some impressive arm strength and was also able to pick up yardage with his legs. Whichever quarterback is under center Sunday, the Buccaneers will continue their search for a more productive passing game to pair with their dominant rushing attack, but they will do so against a Lions' defense that is tied for 28th in passing yards allowed.

Backfield Committee? – Speaking of that dominant rushing attack, it has largely been carried by Irving, though Gainwell and Sean Tucker have fared well with their more limited opportunities. Despite a frame that is not typical of a workhorse back, Irving is averaging 18.6 carries per game, which is fourth in the NFL, and that has gone up to a whopping 23.7 per game over the Bucs' last three outings. Head Coach Todd Bowles conceded that he and his staff would be using the bye week to consider ways to lighten the load on Irving so he stays fresh and healthy for the full season. Will those plans begin to manifest themselves as soon as this week, and what will that mean for Gainwell and Tucker. Gainwell has turned 63 carries into 305 yards, averaging 4.8 per attempt, and also has 15 catches for 121 yards. Tucker has only gotten 15 hands but he has turned them into 80 yards (5.3 avg.) and two touchdowns. Bowles generally subscribes to the "hot hand" philosophy in his backfield and is unlikely to scale things back too much with Irving if the shifty back is on another heater, but there is room to make that backfield into something more of a committee without losing its overall effectiveness.

Another Huge Challenge for Bucs' Rising Defense – The last time the Bucs were on the field, their defense surrendered touchdowns to Caleb Williams and the Bears on Chicago's first two drives. After that, the Bucs clamped down and the Bears never found the end zone again though they held on for a three-point victory. The Bucs have had some impressive performances this season against the likes of Bijan Robinson, Christian Watson, CeeDee Lamb, Jaylen Warren, D'Andre Swift and Luther Burden, but they perhaps have not faced an offense with so many explosive weapons as the Lions. Tampa Bay's top-ranked run defense may be able to slow down the NFL's leading rusher, but it also has to worry about what Gibbs will do in the passing attack (41 catches for 384 yards and two touchdowns). If the Bucs focus their coverage on limiting Goff's hookups with St. Brown they may open up opportunities for big-play specialist Jameson Williams and a tight end in LaPorta who can stretch the seams. And all of this will take place in the thunderously loud Ford Field, where Detroit is already 5-0 this season with three games in which it scored 31 or more points.

Keeping Pace in the South – The Bucs may be tempted to do some scoreboard watching during their game Sunday, because while the Falcons are on a bye the Panthers and Saints also both play in the early-afternoon window. After the Panthers won a road game showdown between those two teams in Week 10 to secure first place in the NFC South, they now get to return home to take on the Baltimore Ravens. Baltimore looked like a strong AFC contender early in the season with a 4-1 start but is now riding a five-game losing streak and is without the straw that stirs their drink, Lamar Jackson. The Ravens will be coming off a dispiriting weekend in which they gave the L.A. Chargers their first win of the season. If the Panthers, who are favored by 2.5 points, can take down the Ravens the Bucs will need a concurrent win against the Lions to avoid falling two games back in the division ahead of a visit from Carolina to Tampa in Week 12. The Saints, who fell to 3-6 with their loss to Carolina get a tough draw in Week 11 as they head to Chicago to take on the 7-2 Bears, winners of four in a row. The Falcons took a 3-7 record into their bye week. The Buccaneers have the second-easiest remaining slate of games based on strength of schedule (combined records of the teams they will be facing), but that run starts with one of the most difficult post-bye challenges in Detroit.

KEY MATCHUPS

1. Lions WR Amon-Ra St. Brown vs. Buccaneers DB Keionte Scott

The Lions use their top receiver, who is an elite route runner, all over their formation, and that includes giving him 34% of his snaps out of the slot. While St. Brown is actually getting the highest percentage of his targets on the outside in his career this season, there will still be plenty of moments when he is the primary responsibility of Scott, the Buccaneers' rookie slot defender. St. Brown leads the Lions with 65 catches for 755 yards and seven touchdowns, ranking in the NFL's top 10 in all three categories. He is also 12th in the NFL with 336 yards after the catch, which make up 44.5% of his overall yardage total. He easily creates separation, rarely drops the ball and even is a tough and willing run blocker. Scott has handled the slot job quite well in his rookie campaign, racking 35 tackles, one sack, two tackles for loss, two quarterback hits and four passes defensed. He has the quick change-of-direction skills that are absolutely crucial to operating in the slot and he has a nose for the football and an all-out attack approach at all times. Scott is also an excellent blitzer and actually leads all NFL defensive backs with five quarterback pressures, all five of which were "quick" pressures, meaning he got to the quarterback in under 2.5 seconds. Both St. Brown and Scott play with a very physical approach, which should make their one-on-one moments very entertaining.

2. Buccaneers RB Bucky Irving vs. Lions LB Derrick Barnes

Even if the Bucs do try to scale Irving's workload back to some small degree, it is still absolutely crucial that they get him going on Sunday in order to keep the chains moving and thus keep Detroit's offense off the field as much as possible. Irving has completely regained the form that made him a rookie sensation in 2024 and is on pace for 1,759 yards from scrimmage and 15 total touchdowns. Irving is a master at taking small increases, accelerating on a dime and then making would-be defenders miss; 273 of his 825 rushing yards have come after he has forced a missed a tackle, which is the fourth most in the NFL. Barnes 40 tackles on the season, and 23 of those have come on running plays, while four of his six tackles for loss have came against runs. He also has 3.0 sacks on the season, which means Irving will occasionally be the one on defense when he's kept in to block. Barnes's responsibilities in the middle of the Lions' defense have only increased since the frightening injury that ended the season for Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell, the team's leading tackler. Like the Bucs' Josiah Trotter, Barnes is a downhill run-stuffer who sheds blocks and quickly fills gaps in the line. The Buccaneers also have reason to remember what Barnes can do, as he was the Lion who came up with the late interception that halted Tampa Bay's comeback in the 2023 Divisional Round playoff game at Ford Field.

3. Lions T Blake Miller vs. Buccaneers OLB Rueben Bain Jr.

A pair of rookie first-round draft picks will be paired up in this battle, as Bain most commonly lines up on the left end of the Bucs' defensive front, which will make him the responsibility of Miller, who is already entrenched as the Lions' starting right tackle. Bain may be heating up as the season progresses, as suggested by his multiple pressures on the Bears' Caleb Williams in Week Nine as well as his game-changing forced fumble in the fourth quarter. Bain is a relentless rusher with tremendous bend and a well-developed arsenal of pass rush moves and the Bucs were beyond thrilled when they were able to land him with the 15th overall pick in April. The Lions were on the clock two picks later and snared Clemson's Miller, allowing them to ably enact their plan of moving on from long-time left tackle Taylor Decker and moving All-Pro right tackle to the left side. Through the first half-season of his career, Miller has looked stronger in pass protection than run blocking and according to Pro Football Focus has only been credited with allowing one sack this season. The Lions like to put their blockers on the move and Miller moves fluidly and times his blocks well to create instant seams for Gibbs. His wide wing span and strong hands allow him to wall off and lock onto blockers before they can get anywhere near Goff in the backfield.

4. Buccaneers G Ben Bredeson vs. Lions DL Alim McNeill

As noted above, Aidan Hutchinson was leading the team and second in the NFL with 50 quarterback pressures at the time of his season-ending knee injury last, but it's actually interior lineman Alim McNeill who leads the Lions in sacks, with 6.5. That's already a career-high for McNeill, who had one sack in 10 games last season. He also has career highs in QB pressures (35) and quick pressures (13). He is also coming off one of his best games of the season, as he recorded six pressures and three quick pressures last Week in the win over New England. All three of his quick pressures came against the Patriots' left guard, Greg Van Roten, and that's the same position that Bredeson manages for the Buccaneers. After a slow start to the season, Tampa Bay's offensive line has begun to round back into its 2024 form, when it had the same five starters as now, including Bredeson. Bredeson had won the left guard spot in training camp before the season and had played so well that the Buccaneers quickly re-signed him to a multi-year deal after that campaign. He's a cerebral, barrel-chested blocker who works well in tandem with Wirfs and center Graham Barton. Bredeson will combine with those two to keep McNeill away from the quarterback if they can.

title: Lions' Dan Campbell refuses to be a 'miserable piece of (expletive)' after string of injuries
description:
Aidan Hutchinson’s season-ending ACL tear is the latest in a long string of Detroit Lions defenders suffering major injuries.
The knee injury is Hutchinson’s second season-ender in three campaigns.
Kerby Joseph is set to finally return after a lengthy absence due to a knee injury.
Lions coach Dan Campbell was asked on Tuesday if he ever laments the bad fortune.
Hutchinson’s injury is devastating for the Detroit defense, which was just beginning to improve after an awful start to the season.
text:
Aidan Hutchinson’s season-ending ACL tear is the latest in a long string of Detroit Lions defenders suffering major injuries.

The knee injury is Hutchinson’s second season-ender in three campaigns. Jack Campbell is out with a serious neck injury suffered earlier this month. Brian Branch just recently returned from a torn Achilles. Kerby Joseph is set to finally return after a lengthy absence due to a knee injury. Alim McNeill tore his ACL in 2024.

Detroit’s defense hasn’t been at full strength in years. It might never be.

Lions coach Dan Campbell was asked on Tuesday if he ever laments the bad fortune.

“I think there's times where if you’re not careful, you lay in bed at night and you start thinking about all the ‘what ifs?’” Campbell said. “And at some point, you become a miserable piece of s---. And I’m not going to do it, man. We’re not doing it. I refuse to look at it that way.”

Campbell’s mentality is the only one to take. To wallow in the losses would be to punt on the rest of the season.

“Does it stink?” he said. “It sure did in the moment. It's time to move on. We have to. And what has happened with Jack Campbell and with Hutch now will not be in vain. We can't allow it to. They got us to this point. And so, what are we going to do about it, man? Are we just going to let it go to waste or are we going to do something and pick up the slack?”

Campbell was asked whether he'd attempt to curtail celebrations after Hutchinson's injury.

"No, I don't believe that," he said. "I think what happened speaks for itself. We're not talking to 8-year-olds here."

Hutchinson’s injury is devastating for the Detroit defense, which was just beginning to improve after an awful start to the season. Hutchinson leads the Lions with 50 QB pressures; the next closest is McNeill with 35. The nearest edge rusher is D.J. Wonnum with 22.

There is no replacing an Aidan Hutchinson. Campbell knows he’ll need the collective to step up if the Lions are going to survive in the toughest division in football.

“Does it hurt?” Campbell said. “Absolutely. It's just going to require more of the other guys around him. It's going to require more offensively. It's going to require more on special teams. And we are capable of all that. It's about finding a way to win.”

The best way for the Lions to find wins without Hutchinson: Lean even more on an already explosive offense.

text:
The Kansas City Chiefs cruised past the Atlanta Falcons in Week 10, as they posted a 35-13 victory when all was said and done. While the Falcons haven't been all that consistent this season, this very well may have been the Chiefs' most impressive win of the year. Not only was the passing game firing on all cylinders, but they managed to demolish Atlanta without star running back Kenneth Walker III on the field.

Walker suffered a groin injury late last week that ultimately prevented him from playing against the Falcons, and while his team ultimately didn't need him, it is well aware that it is going to need its top offensive playmaker healthy and on the field as the second half of the season gets underway. The hope has always been that Walker would only have to miss one game with this injury, with one NFL insider providing an update on his status ahead of Week 11.

Chiefs Hopeful That Kenneth Walker III Can Return to Practice This Week

After winning Super Bowl LX MVP with the Seattle Seahawks, Walker signed with the Chiefs in free agency on a three-year, $43.05 million contract, and he has quickly proven to be one of the best signings across the league in recent memory. Through eight games, Walker has run for 872 yards and seven touchdowns on 159 carries, while also catching 26 passes for 172 yards and four more scores.

It's been a change of pace for Kansas City on offense, as it has gone from leaning on Patrick Mahomes and its aerial attack to making Walker the focal point of its offense in the blink of an eye. Being without him against the Falcons would seemingly have created a big issue for this team, but rookie Emmett Johnson stepped in and turned in the sort of outing Walker has become known for this season (22 CAR, 101 YDS, 6 REC, 70 YDS, 2 TD).

Johnson has quickly proven he can hold his own while filling in for Walker, but it's clear the latter option is the guy who can help the Chiefs make a deep playoff run immediately this year. Right now, the primary objective involves getting Walker back on the field, with NFL insider Ian Rapoport of NFL Network revealing that the team is "hopeful" that he can practice on Wednesday.

"My understanding, the groin injury for Kenneth Walker, minor. The hope was keep him out last week, somehow make do with a rookie most people have never heard of taken in the mid rounds, and have him back the following week," Rapoport said on "Big Day." "That is the hope, that he is back at practice tomorrow and that he is able to play."

Chiefs Don't Necessarily Have to Rush Kenneth Walker III Back From Injury

Kansas City is in a unique spot when it comes to Walker's injury status, thanks in large part to how effective Johnson has been this season. In Week 11, the Chiefs will be playing the lowly Arizona Cardinals, before turning around and taking on the high-powered Buffalo Bills on Thanksgiving Day. Depending on how Walker feels, K.C. could conceivably give Walker another week to get healthy before having him return for the Buffalo matchup.

If Walker is healthy and good to go, though, there's really no reason to hold him out, and the Chiefs clearly want him back on the field as soon as he gets the green light from their medical staff. As is always the case, Walker's availability for Sunday will depend on what he can do at practice throughout the week, but as of right now, it seems like he has a decent shot at returning after a one-game absence.

text:
Washington Commanders defensive end Deatrich Wise Jr. said players should decide for themselves whether to use riskier celebrations after Detroit Lions star Aidan Hutchinson tore his ACL while celebrating a sack.

"Every player has their own style of celebration," Wise said in an interview with OutKick. "Some players have more of a riskier celebration than others, and those with the riskier celebrations, I think that I’ll leave that one up to them whether they want to continue it or not."

Hutchinson injured his right knee after leaping in celebration of a sack against the New England Patriots in Munich on Nov. 15. The Lions later confirmed he had a torn ACL, ending his season.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

DAN CAMPBELL WON'T STOP PLAYERS FROM CELEBRATING EVEN AFTER STAR AIDAN HUTCHINSON WAS INJURED CELEBRATING

Wise, who said he keeps his own celebrations simple, has a routine inspired by fencing.

"I have a fencing celebration after my sack," he said. "I like pull the sword out and then I start fencing with it, like on guard. I put it back in."

Wise said he fenced in seventh grade and connected the sport’s strategy to playing defensive end.

"Fencing is … like human chess in a sense," he said. "It’s all about leverage. It’s all about knowing the person in front of you, also knowing yourself."

He said he had not fenced regularly since childhood, though he had the opportunity to do it again a few months before the interview.

Wise returns after quad injury

Wise is sharing his message about the potential injury risks of certain celebrations after recently working his way back from a devastating injury himself, having missed almost the entire 2025 season after suffering a torn left quadriceps/quad tendon requiring season-ending surgery after players rolled up on his leg on a point-after try last September.

Now, he will play in his second primetime game in as many weeks, as he prepares for Washington’s Monday-night game against the Cincinnati Bengals. He had already returned to the field in the Commanders’ Nov. 12 win over the New York Giants, after missing most of the last year with the injury.

Washington activated Wise from the reserve/physically unable to perform list in October. In the Giants game, he helped stop quarterback Jameis Winston for a one-yard gain near the goal line. The Commanders won 24–21 on a late touchdown pass from Jayden Daniels to Stefon Diggs.

Asked what he could bring to Washington’s defense, Wise said he would continue to bring "my aggressiveness, my power, and my ability to play up and down the line of scrimmage."

He said the team’s biggest improvement would come from playing together and maintaining a high level for all four quarters.

Wise Up Foundation promotes trades and supports veterans

Wise wore a cleat representing his Wise Up Foundation, whose mission he described as providing educational opportunities, uniting communities, supporting students and student-athletes, and honoring military veterans.

One of the foundation’s programs, Bridge 2 Trades, introduces high school students to skilled trades through hands-on learning, career exploration and mentorship. The organization says its program includes exposure to areas such as plumbing, electrical work and carpentry.

Wise said he believes students hear more about four-year colleges than about trade careers.

"There’s nothing wrong with colleges," he said. "There’s nothing wrong with going to school, getting a four-year degree, but I also want to educate people and kids on that there’s other options outside of college."

He said trade skills can give people a path to financial independence, starting a business or hiring people in their communities. Wise also said people can earn "six, seven figures" in trades. The interview did not specify which careers, experience levels or locations he was referring to.

The foundation also works with veterans. Wise said he wants to help veterans understand what benefits may be available through the Department of Veterans Affairs and assist with their transition back into civilian life.

His military ties are personal. Wise said his mother is an Army major and that relatives have served across multiple branches. The Patriots previously reported that his mother served 22 years in the Army as a military nurse. The Wise Up Foundation says its "Hot Meals for Vets" program began in 2020 and has served homeless and disabled veterans.

NONPROFIT OFFERS VETERANS SECOND CAREER THROUGH COMMERCIAL DRONE PILOT TRAINING

‘An opportunity to play football again’

Asked whether the Commanders’ military identity encouraged him to sign with the team, Wise said it did not.

"No, it was just an opportunity to play football again," he said.

He added that playing in Washington is an honor because the team’s platform can reach and inspire people. Wise recalled a visit to Walter Reed National Military Medical Center about three weeks before the interview, where he met service members and heard about the role football played in their lives.

"They all was telling me how they all have different NFL favorite players, favorite teams," Wise said. "You could just hear the joy in their voice talking about the games they watched when they was overseas and how much it meant to them."

He said he hoped to use his platform "to inspire, to bring joy to someone who’s watching the game."

Lessons from New England

Wise won a Super Bowl with the New England Patriots, where he played under Bill Belichick and alongside quarterback Tom Brady. Asked what he had brought from that experience to Washington, he pointed to team chemistry and execution.

"Championship football comes down to the chemistry that is done off the field and then playing high-level football on the field," he said, adding that players need to manage the relationship between the pass rush and coverage and be ready when their number is called.

Wise said the Commanders watch film and break down opponents together, and described the team as a family and a brotherhood.

He also recalled Brady telling him to focus on making perfect throws in practice and treat each practice like game day. Wise said he applies that lesson to his own position by working on "having perfect hands."

Asked to compare Belichick and Commanders coach Dan Quinn, Wise said both emphasize toughness, mindset, focus and self-improvement.

"They bring different things to the game to achieve the same thing," he said.

Washington’s playoff hopes

The interview took place after Washington’s win over the Giants, which Wise described as part of the team’s daily effort to win.

"We build a great, great brotherhood," he said. "Dan Quinn’s been teaching that since day one."

At the time, Washington was 3–5–1 and third in the NFC East, behind the 5–3–1 Giants and 4–6 Dallas Cowboys. The Commanders were still in contention, though the standings left little room for error.

text:
Injuries can quickly derail an NFL campaign. The Eagles have fallen victim to that notion in 2026, losing several starters during a disappointing seven-game losing streak. Returning to full health will be crucial to snapping the skid and being competitive in the second half of the season.

The Eagles' Week 10 bye provided extra rest for sidelined players ahead of a matchup against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Week 11. The team's first injury report of the week will be released following Wednesday's practice.

For now, let's take a peek at those on the mend in the City of Brotherly Love.

Eagles who could return in Week 11

DeVonta Smith, WR

The Eagles have been without wide receiver DeVonta Smith for five of their nine games, as he deals with a hamstring injury. Philadelphia has been careful in this situation for a reason. Hamstring issues can be especially tricky for pass-catchers who rely on acceleration and change of direction in routes.

The news surrounding Smith is trending in the right direction ahead of Week 11. The Eagles released wide receiver Hollywood Brown, suggesting the team is banking on Smith being back on the field soon. The 28-year-old has tallied 310 yards and two touchdowns on 26 receptions (41 targets).

Dontayvion Wicks, WR

Smith isn't the only wide receiver Eagles fans are anxiously awaiting to recover. Dontayvion Wicks sustained an ankle injury in the fourth quarter of Philadelphia's Week 6 loss to the Panthers. The hope is that four weeks of rest are enough to get the exciting offseason acquisition back in the lineup.

Pay attention to Smith and Wicks's status on Wednesday's injury report. Even limited participation would be a big step toward playing on Sunday afternoon. Their returns would be a notable boost for quarterback Joe Milton. He completed 18 of 34 passes for 169 yards in his Eagles debut in Week 9.

Jihaad Campbell, LB

Linebacker Jihaad Campbell played 37 snaps against the Cowboys in Week 7 before he needed to be replaced due to hamstring and quad injuries. The Alabama product was then sidelined in Week 8 and Week 9. A return to practice, in any fashion, will be the first step to getting Campbell back on the field.

Campbell's absence has opened the door for Jeremiah Trotter Jr. to play an every-down role at linebacker. He led the Eagles with 11 tackles (three tackles for loss) in Week 9's loss to the Giants. Keep an eye on how defensive coordinator Vic Fangio splits linebacker snaps once Campbell recovers.

Michael Carter II, S

Defensive back Michael Carter II suffered an abdominal strain in Week 5. The veteran returned to play in Week 8 but aggravated the injury in one snap. There hasn't been a concrete update on his status, other than the fact that he did not practice prior to being ruled out in Week 9. Expect clarity this week.

Carter allowed a 56.3 passer rating when targeted and just 5.5 yards per reception before going down (per PFF). His return would be welcomed in a secondary that has been subpar as of late. Safety Andrew Mukuba is missing tackles, while cornerback Kenny Moore II is struggling in coverage.

Britain Covey, WR

Return specialist Britain Covey sustained a knee injury on Week 7's opening kickoff. He did not return to the game or practice before Philly's bye. Covey was not placed on injured reserve, though, so his activation should be near. Makai Lemon and Cooper DeJean will field kicks/punts in the meantime.

Eagles who remain on IR

Quarterback Jalen Hurts was placed on injured reserve on Oct. 17 and isn't expected to return this season. The three-time Pro Bowler suffered a calf injury in Week 4, which caused severe blood clots to form. Those clots moved to his lungs. Hurts is under contract with the Eagles through 2028.

Philadelphia has opened the 21-day practice window for running back Will Shipley. The third-year pro had logged 88 total yards and one touchdown on 25 touches before going down with a foot injury. Fellow running back Tank Bigsby does not yet have a timetable to heal from a core muscle issue.

Other members of the Eagles' IR list include WR Johnny Wilson (knee), S Andre' Sam (foot) and S Tucker Large (knee).

title: Why Lions' Dan Campbell refuses to be a 'miserable piece of [expletive]' - Detroit Free Press
description:
Star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson is out for the season after tearing his ACL, his third major leg injury.
Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, Jack Campbell, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph were in the starting lineup that afternoon against the Dallas Cowboys.
Right before he did, Joseph was sidelined with a chronic knee injury that has kept him out for the past 13 months.
The hope was that when Joseph eventually returned this season, the rest of the Lions’ defensive core would be right beside him.
For Hutchinson, this is the third major leg injury he has suffered in the last seven seasons.
text:
The Detroit Lions have been plagued by injuries to their five best defensive players since October 2024.

Star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson is out for the season after tearing his ACL, his third major leg injury.

The last time the Detroit Lions had their five best defensive players on the field at the same time was Oct. 13, 2024. Aidan Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, Jack Campbell, Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph were in the starting lineup that afternoon against the Dallas Cowboys. Early in the third quarter of that 47-9 victory, Hutchinson fractured his left fibula and tibia on a sack of Dak Prescott. The Lions’ defense hasn’t been at full strength since.

McNeill suffered a torn anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee later that year. He didn’t return to action until the following October. Right before he did, Joseph was sidelined with a chronic knee injury that has kept him out for the past 13 months. During the extended period Joseph hasn't played, Branch ruptured the Achilles tendon in his right leg last December, Campbell suffered a serious neck injury on Nov. 1 that has kept him hospitalized for more than two weeks, and Hutchinson went down yet again – this time tearing the ACL in his right knee while celebrating a sack in the first quarter of the Lions’ win over New England in Germany this past Sunday.

Hutchinson’s latest setback, another season-ender, coincidentally came just days before the Lions began making preparations to activate Joseph for the first time this year ahead of the team's upcoming showdown with Tampa Bay. Branch, of course, already has rejoined the fold, having played in the last four games.

The hope was that when Joseph eventually returned this season, the rest of the Lions’ defensive core would be right beside him. But that won’t come to pass, leaving some people lamenting the team’s bad luck and wondering just how good the 7-2 Lions would be if Hutchinson, McNeill, Campbell, Branch and Joseph were all available right now.

Lions coach Dan Campbell is not one of them.

“I think there are times where if you’re not careful, you lay in bed at night and you start thinking about all the ‘what ifs?’” Campbell said Tuesday, Nov. 17. “And at some point, you become a miserable piece of [expletive]. And I’m not going to do it, man. We’re not doing it. I refuse to look it that way.”

Instead, Campbell is taking a resolute approach in the aftermath of Hutchinson’s injury.

“Does it stink?” he said. “It sure did in the moment. It's time to move on. We have to. And what has happened with Jack Campbell and with Hutch now will not be in vain. We can't allow it to. They got us to this point. And so, what are we going to do about it, man? Are we just going to let it go to waste or are we going to do something and pick up the slack?”

Campbell is betting that Hutchinson’s teammates will do the latter. But losing Hutchinson, the Lions’ top pass rusher, is a devastating blow. After all, he has produced the second-most pressures – 52 – in the NFL this season, according to Pro Football Focus. He also played 82% of the team’s defensive snaps. Only safety Chuck Clark and linebacker Derrick Barnes have been on the field more than Hutchinson.

“One guy cannot pick up the slack of Aidan Hutchinson, but we have enough here to weather this storm and rise above it,” Campbell said. “So, we'll do that.”

As the Lions move forward without their star edge defender, Hutchinson faces a long road to recovery. Campbell said Hutchinson, who is expected to undergo surgery within the next two weeks, may have incurred more damage to the knee than just a torn ACL. For Hutchinson, this is the third major leg injury he has suffered in the last seven seasons. He fractured his right ankle during his junior year at Michigan in 2020 and then broke his left leg in 2024 during Year 3 with the Lions. Now, barely 12 months after he signed $180 million contract extension, Hutchinson’s football career has been derailed once again.

“It's unfortunate,” Campbell said. “I hate it for him. Certainly for us being selfish, it's hard for us, too, just to swallow it right when it happens.”

But he is also not wallowing in self pity.

“Does it hurt?” Campbell said. “Absolutely. It's just going to require more of other guys around him. It's going to require more offensively. It's going to require more on special teams. And we are capable of all that. It's about finding a way to win.”

He and the Lions must try to do that without their five best defensive players on the field at the same time. As difficult as it may be, it’s something they have become accustomed to ever since Oct. 13, 2024.

text:
TEMPE, Ariz. -- Cardinals quarterback Gardner Minshew II had surgery on his right ulnar collateral ligament on Monday, a source told ESPN.

He is expected to make a full recovery, the source said.

Minshew suffered the injury at the end of the first half of Arizona's Week 9 loss at the Seattle Seahawks. He played the second half but didn't realize the severity of his injury.

He was put on injured reserve two days later, ending his first season with the Cardinals. Minshew signed a one-year deal in March and is scheduled to be a free agent after the season.

Last Wednesday, coach Mike LaFleur said Minshew could tell something was wrong after suffering the injury but his adrenaline was pumping so he couldn't tell how bad it truly was. LaFleur said he was surprised by the news of Minshew's injury.

LaFleur said the injury was "devastating" for Minshew.

"Even on Monday, he felt confident that it wasn't that much until the test came back," LaFleur said.

Minshew threw for 354 yards and three touchdowns on 38-of-53 passing in five full quarters, an overtime and about 95 seconds of the third quarter of Arizona's Week 8 win over the Cowboys.

The Houston Texans placed linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, their leading tackler this season, on injured reserve Tuesday, which will sideline him for at least the next four games.

Al-Shaair was inactive for Houston's 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns on Sunday because of a groin injury.

"Not having Azeez is difficult for us. He's the heartbeat of our defense, does a lot for us -- communicating, leading, playing really well for us," coach DeMeco Ryans told reporters Tuesday.

Shaair wears the green dot on his helmet as the player who relays the defensive calls to his teammates on the field. Henry To'oTo'o filled that role last Sunday with Shaair out and will continue in that role, Ryans said Tuesday.

Shaair leads the Texans with 68 tackles in seven games. He also led the team in tackles last season when he had 103 and was a first-time Pro Bowl selection.

In the offseason he signed a three-year, $54 million extension with the Texans.

text:
ALLEN PARK — Kerby Joseph hasn’t played in an NFL game in more than a year.

But Lions coach Dan Campbell says the wait is almost over.

The former All-Pro safety, who led the league with nine interceptions in his last full season in 2024, has been sidelined since October 2025 dealing with a chronic knee injury. But after placing Joseph on the Physically Unable to Perform (PUP) list to start this season, the Lions opened his 21-day acclimation window late last month. And after two weeks of ramped-up activity in practice, Campbell said the plan is to add Joseph to the 53-man roster by the Wednesday, Sept. 18, deadline and have him on the field playing Sunday against Tampa Bay.

“He has done a good job,” Campbell said. “That's why I'm glad we started his clock (three) weeks ago … so that we can ramp him up, get him work, see how the knee responded. He's done a really good job. The knee has responded well. The plan is to get him going. Going to let him play.”

He might play a lot, too. Fellow safety Brian Branch was on a pitch count last month when he made his return following a 10-month recovery from a torn Achilles. He saw limited snaps in the first of half of season debut against Green Bay on Oct. 25, then played the entire second half and has been a mainstay ever since, other than being forced to miss part of his second game (against Minnesota) due to a concussion.

“We started Kerby earlier,” Campbell said. “We were being very conservative with Branch, and probably could have started him a week sooner than we did. But that's why Kerby, (we said) let's start it a week earlier. And if we had to park him for another week on the roster, we’d find a way if he wasn't ready. But at least we got reps on it, right? We got reps. We got time.

“So, is there a pinch count? Yeah, but not like what Branch had his first game. So I think we're going to be able to get a little bit more out of Kirby here.”

How Joseph’s return affects the Lions’ rotation in the secondary remains to be seen, but Branch has been starting alongside veteran Chuck Clark at the safety position.

Since entering the NFL in 2022, Joseph leads the NFL in interceptions with 20, and when he last spoke to reporters he said he was encouraged about how the knee felt. He also sounded like himself.

"I’m still him, I hope y’all ain’t forget,” said Joseph, who turned 26 this past weekend. “I’m still him. Just got to go do some other stuff real quick, but I’m still him."

Injury updates on D.J. Reed, Cade Mays

While Joseph is expected back to face the Buccaneers, Campbell sounded unsure about starting cornerback D.J. Reed, who has missed the Lions' last two games because of a hip injury.

“It's a good question," Campbell said. "I'll know more today. He's improved every week. I can't say for certain that he'll be ready this week though.”

Center Cade Mays (ankle), who has been out since leaving the Minnesota game on Nov. 1 because of an ankle injury, is unlikely to play against the Buccaneers. But Campbell likes what he has seen from Juice Scruggs, who has made seven starts in place of Mays, Detroit's big free-agent signing who missed the first six games because of a broken wrist suffered in training camp.

“I don’t see Cade being ready this week," Campbell said. "There’s a chance, but I’m not putting all my eggs in that basket. And Juice has been doing a nice job for us. He’s playing really good football. That whole o-line played dang good football the other day.”

Lions claim DE Tyrus Wheat

Aidan Hutchinson (torn ACL) likely will be placed on injured reserve to make room on the roster for Joseph's activation Wednesday. But the Lions did make another move Monday to shore up the depth on the defensive line, claiming edge rusher Tyrus Wheat off waivers from Dallas.

It's the second stint in Detroit for Wheat, a fourth-year pro the Lions claimed off waivers — also from Dallas — at the end of the 2025 preseason. He was active for 15 games here last season, playing mostly on special teams.

"We were fired up to get Wheat back because he knows our system," Campbell said. "We liked him. We still like him, obviously. He's got special teams ability and there's things that he does as a rush defensive end that were intriguing to us.

"It was one of those things that didn't work out at the end of last year to get him back, but we liked Wheat. And so, it's good to have him back with us. 'What does that mean this week?' I don't entirely know, but I know it's good to have him because we'll need him at some point, if not now.”

The Lions waived defensive back Nick Whiteside in order to sign Wheat on Monday, but he could be a candidate to return this week as a practice-squad signing.
